mainTopic: Majority (רוב) and the abandoned baby: lineage, saving a life, and practical laws. Then the opening of chapter two on proving a virgin's כתובה.
overview: Just before this passage, רב was reported to rule like רבי יוסי: a girl attacked in a city where most people have proper lineage may still marry a כהן. The גמרא challenges this from a משנה about an abandoned baby, where רב says a majority only helps to keep the baby alive, not for יוחסין. It answers that the girl's case happened among the wagons of ציפורי, where there were two majorities. רב חנן בר רבא's view that it was a one-time emergency ruling must come from a different tradition. Then the גמרא studies the abandoned-baby משנה itself. It moves שמואל's statement so that we clear rubble off the baby on שבת even in a mostly non-Jewish city, because we never follow the majority when a life is at stake. רב פפא and ריש לקיש explain what each clause means in practice: feeding him נבילות, returning his lost item, and paying damages. The first chapter ends with a הדרן. The second chapter opens with a משנה about a widow or divorcee who claims she married as a בתולה, and about רבי יהושע agreeing that a man who says 'this field was your father's and I bought it' is believed.

steps.title: The case of the abandoned baby in a mixed city
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a source: a baby found in a city of Jews and non-Jews follows the majority, and if it is half-and-half, he is treated as Jewish.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone found an abandoned baby in a mixed city: if most people there are non-Jews, the baby is treated as a non-Jew. If most are Jews, he is treated as a Jew. If it is half and half, he is treated as a Jew.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting a source that it will use in the next step to challenge רב's ruling like רבי יוסי. This step sets up that challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On its face, this source simply says that we follow the רוב, the majority of the city, to decide the baby's status. The challenge will come from how רב explains this source in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: An abandoned baby whose parents are unknown
Majority; the rule that we follow what most people are
Half and half; an evenly split population
A non-Jew

phrases.english: If one found in it an abandoned baby,
phrases.notes: "In it" means in a city where both Jews and non-Jews live.

phrases.english: if most are non-Jews, he is a non-Jew.
If most are Jews, he is a Jew.
If half and half, he is a Jew.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source that will be used against רב חייא בר אשי's report of רב's ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An abandoned baby follows the majority of the city; when the city is evenly split, he is treated as Jewish.

steps.title: רב limits the majority to saving the baby's life, not lineage
steps.stepSummary: רב says the source only treats the baby as Jewish to keep him alive, not for lineage. שמואל says it is about clearing rubble off him on שבת. This seems to contradict רב's ruling that one majority is enough for lineage.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב said: The source taught this only for keeping him alive, but not for lineage. And שמואל said: It is for clearing a pile of rubble off him on שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: רב and שמואל both explain that the baby's "Jewish" status here is only for saving his life. This creates a challenge: רב seems to hold that a majority is not enough for lineage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, רב supposedly ruled like רבי יוסי, letting a girl marry a כהן based on a majority. Here רב says a majority does not decide lineage. So how could רב have said one majority is enough for the girl?

keyTerms.meaning: To keep him alive; to give him food and care
Lineage; family status for marriage, such as marrying a Jew or a כהן
To clear a pile of rubble, even on שבת, to save a life

steps.confusionAlert: Neither רב nor שמואל is saying the baby is not Jewish at all. They are saying the majority only works for saving his life. For lineage, the majority is not enough on its own.

phrases.english: And רב said:
They taught this only for keeping him alive,
but for lineage, no.
And שמואל said:
It is to clear the rubble pile off him.
phrases.notes: He means digging him out on שבת, which is allowed to save a life.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא לְהַחְיוֹתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses רב's explanation of the source from step 1 to challenge the claim that רב ruled like רבי יוסי.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חייא בר אשי's report that רב ruled like רבי יוסי, allowing marriage to a כהן based on a majority.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Here רב says a majority does not decide lineage, so he could not have allowed a girl into כהונה based on one majority.

steps.title: The original case had two majorities, in the wagons of ציפורי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רב ירמיה forgot רב's statement that the girl's case happened among the wagons of ציפורי, where there were two majorities.
steps.simpleTranslation: He forgot what רב יהודה said in the name of רב: The incident happened among the wagons of ציפורי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It says the one who asked forgot a detail: the girl's case happened in a place where there were two majorities, not just one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Among the wagons of ציפורי, both the people living in the city and the travelers passing through were mostly of proper lineage. So רב can agree that one majority is not enough for lineage. The girl was allowed because there were תרי רובי (two majorities).

keyTerms.meaning: It slipped his mind; he forgot
Wagons; the busy wagon market area
ציפורי, a major city in the Galilee
An actual incident

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב, one majority is not enough for lineage, but two majorities are. The girl's case in ציפורי had two majorities.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the rule for lineage is stricter than for saving a life: a single רוב is not enough, and you need two.

phrases.english: This slipped his mind,
phrases.notes: "He" is רב ירמיה, who raised the challenge.

phrases.english: what רב יהודה said in the name of רב:
The incident happened among the wagons of ציפורי.
phrases.notes: There, both the residents and the passing travelers were mostly of good lineage, so there were two majorities.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִשְׁתְּמִיטְתֵּיהּ הָא דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 2 by redefining the original case as one with two majorities.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the facts were different from what the questioner assumed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The girl was allowed into כהונה based on one majority, which contradicts רב's view on the baby.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case had two majorities, residents and travelers, so it does not contradict רב's rule that one majority is not enough for lineage.

steps.title: A problem for רב חנן בר רבא's 'emergency ruling' view
steps.stepSummary: רב חנן בר רבא said the ruling allowing the girl was a one-time emergency ruling. If there really were two majorities, why would an emergency ruling be needed?
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רב חנן בר רבא, who said it was a one-time emergency ruling, is this not difficult?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new difficulty. It points to another opinion about the girl's case that does not seem to fit the two-majorities answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the case had two majorities, the girl should be allowed by the normal rules. Then why would רב חנן בר רבא call it a הוראת שעה, a special ruling just for that time? His view seems to clash with the ציפורי explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: A one-time ruling for special circumstances, not the normal rule
It is difficult; there is a problem here

phrases.english: And according to רב חנן בר רבא, who said:
It was a one-time emergency ruling,
is this not difficult?
phrases.notes: If there were two majorities, the girl would be allowed normally, so why call it an emergency ruling?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְרַב חָנָן בַּר רָבָא, דְּאָמַר: הוֹרָאַת שָׁעָה הָיְתָה, קַשְׁיָא הָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 3 using another tradition about the same case.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the ציפורי case had two majorities.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two majorities would allow the girl under normal rules, so calling the ruling a הוראת שעה makes no sense if the case had two majorities.

steps.title: Two different traditions about the same case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that whoever teaches the 'emergency ruling' version does not teach the ציפורי version. In his view there was only one majority, and the girl was allowed only because of the special circumstances.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who teaches this does not teach that.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the difficulty by saying these are two separate traditions that do not go together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חנן בר רבא does not accept that the case happened in the wagons of ציפורי. In his version there was only one majority, which normally is not enough for lineage. So the permission had to be a special emergency ruling, which still fits רב's view on the baby.

keyTerms.meaning: The one who teaches this tradition
Does not teach that other tradition

steps.whatToRemember: Both traditions agree with רב that one majority is normally not enough for lineage. One says the case had two majorities. The other says it had one majority and was allowed only as a special one-time ruling.

phrases.english: The one who teaches this,
phrases.notes: "This" is the emergency-ruling statement of רב חנן בר רבא.

phrases.english: does not teach that.
phrases.notes: "That" is רב יהודה's statement that the case happened among the wagons of ציפורי.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן דְּמַתְנֵי הָא, לָא מַתְנֵי הָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves step 4 by separating the two traditions.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the traditions: two separate versions of the same case that do not go together.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב חנן בר רבא's emergency ruling clashes with the two-majorities explanation.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב חנן בר רבא holds there was only one majority, so a special ruling was needed. This is still consistent with רב's view that one majority is not enough for lineage.

steps.title: Going back to the baby משנה itself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה of the abandoned baby again, together with the dispute of רב and שמואל, so it can now study the ruling on its own terms.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now let's look at the source itself: if someone found an abandoned baby in a mixed city, then if most people there are non-Jews, he is a non-Jew. If most are Jews, he is a Jew. If it is half and half, he is a Jew. רב said: this was taught only to keep him alive, but not for lineage. שמואל said: it was taught for clearing a pile of rubble off him on שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: Until now the משנה was used only for the question about majorities and lineage. Now the גמרא says 'גופה' and goes back to study the משנה for its own sake. This sets up the questions that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to here this is the same text as before, but now it serves a new purpose: it is the starting point for a fresh look at the ruling. רב limits 'he is a Jew' to keeping him alive, not to יוחסין. שמואל ties the half-and-half ruling to clearing rubble on שבת, which is פיקוח נפש.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The thing itself.' The גמרא returns to examine a source it quoted earlier.
An abandoned baby whose parents are unknown
Half and half (an even split)
To clear away a pile of rubble to save someone, even on שבת

phrases.english: The matter itself:
If one found an abandoned baby in it,
phrases.notes: 'In it' means a city where both Jews and non-Jews live.

phrases.english: if most are non-Jews, he is a non-Jew;
if most are Jews, he is a Jew;
if half and half, he is a Jew.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא לְהַחְיוֹתוֹ,
phrases.english: רב said: they taught this only to keep him alive,
but for lineage, no.

phrases.aramaic: וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: לְפַקֵּחַ עָלָיו אֶת הַגַּל.
phrases.english: And שמואל said: it is for clearing the rubble off him.
phrases.notes: This means on שבת, when clearing rubble is normally forbidden unless a life is at stake.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the lineage discussion and opens a fresh study of the משנה itself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An abandoned baby follows the city's majority, and in a half-and-half city he is treated as a Jew. רב says this is only to keep him alive. שמואל says it is for clearing rubble on שבת.

steps.title: Does שמואל follow a majority for saving a life?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges שמואל: he himself said we never follow the majority in matters of saving a life.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did שמואל really say that? But רב יוסף said in the name of רב יהודה, who said in the name of שמואל: in matters of saving a life, we do not follow the majority!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how שמואל could say this, because it clashes with another statement of his.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If שמואל connects clearing rubble to the half-and-half case, it sounds like we would not clear it when most of the city is non-Jewish. That means following the majority in a life-or-death case. But שמואל himself ruled that in פיקוח נפש we never follow the majority.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Did he really say that?' This opens a challenge from the same person's other words.
Saving a life, which pushes aside almost every מצוה
We do not follow the majority

phrases.english: And did שמואל really say this?
But didn't רב יוסף say
that רב יהודה said that שמואל said:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין הוֹלְכִין בְּפִיקּוּחַ נֶפֶשׁ אַחַר הָרוֹב!
phrases.english: We do not follow the majority in saving a life!

steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's statement that the half-and-half ruling is about clearing rubble
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Linking life-saving to the half-and-half case implies no rescue when the majority is non-Jewish. That would mean following the majority in פיקוח נפש, which contradicts שמואל's own rule.

steps.title: שמואל's statement belongs on the first clause
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא moves שמואל's statement to the first clause: even when most of the city is non-Jewish, we still clear the rubble off the baby.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, when שמואל's statement was said, it was said on the first clause: 'if most are non-Jews, he is a non-Jew.' שמואל said: but for clearing rubble off him, that is not so.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that we misplaced שמואל's words. He was really commenting on the majority-non-Jewish case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל was not explaining the half-and-half ruling. He was limiting the first clause: the baby counts as a non-Jew, but not when it comes to saving his life. So even with a non-Jewish majority we clear the rubble, which fits his rule that we don't follow the majority in פיקוח נפש.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Rather, when it was said...' This moves a statement to a different place.
On the first clause
It is not so (the rule does not apply here)

steps.whatToRemember: In saving a life, the majority does not matter. Even in a mostly non-Jewish city we clear the rubble off an unknown baby on שבת.

phrases.english: Rather, when שמואל's statement was said,
it was said on the first clause:
'if most are non-Jews, he is a non-Jew.'

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: וּלְפַקֵּחַ עָלָיו אֶת הַגַּל
phrases.english: שמואל said: but as for clearing the rubble off him,
it is not so.
phrases.notes: He means we do not treat him as a non-Jew here; we still clear the rubble to save him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא כִּי אִיתְּמַר דִּשְׁמוּאֵל אַרֵישָׁא אִתְּמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 7 by moving שמואל's statement.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Relocating a statement to a different clause
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שמואל was explaining that the half-and-half ruling is about clearing rubble.
steps.terutzMaskana: שמואל was limiting the first clause: even with a non-Jewish majority, we clear the rubble.

steps.title: What does 'he is a non-Jew' mean in practice?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical law follows from calling the baby a non-Jew when most of the city is non-Jewish.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If most are non-Jews, he is a non-Jew.' For what law does this matter?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question. It sets up רב פפא's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We now know he is not treated as a non-Jew for saving his life. So the גמרא wants to know where this label does make a difference.

keyTerms.meaning: 'For what law?' What practical difference does this make?

phrases.english: 'If most are non-Jews, he is a non-Jew.'
For what law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After limiting the clause in Step 8, asks where the clause does apply.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical result of treating the baby as a non-Jew

steps.title: We may feed him non-kosher food
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers: calling him a non-Jew means we may feed him נבילות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: it means we may feed him non-kosher meat.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives the practical difference for the non-Jewish-majority case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since he follows the non-Jewish majority, we don't have to keep him away from forbidden food. This is an ordinary matter, not life and death, so following the majority works here.

keyTerms.meaning: Meat of animals that were not slaughtered properly; non-kosher food

phrases.english: רב פפא said: to feed him non-kosher meat.

steps.title: What does 'he is a Jew' mean in practice?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks the same question about the Jewish-majority clause.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If most are Jews, he is a Jew.' For what law does this matter?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks the same clarifying question about the second clause, setting up רב פפא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב already said this label does not decide his lineage. So the גמרא asks which other law it affects.

phrases.english: 'If most are Jews, he is a Jew.'
For what law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same question as Step 9, now on the second clause.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical result of treating the baby as a Jew

steps.title: We must return his lost item
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers: calling him a Jew means we must return a lost object to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: it means we must return a lost object to him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives the practical difference for the Jewish-majority case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מצוה of returning lost property applies to a fellow Jew. Following the Jewish majority, this baby gets that protection.

keyTerms.meaning: The מצוה of returning a lost object to its owner

steps.whatToRemember: The majority decides everyday matters, like feeding him נבילות or returning his lost item. It does not decide matters of saving a life, and according to רב it does not decide lineage.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: לְהַחְזִיר לוֹ אֲבֵידָה.
phrases.english: רב פפא said: to return a lost object to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: לְהַחְזִיר לוֹ אֲבֵידָה
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: We must return his lost property to him.

steps.title: What law follows from the half-and-half case?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ruling that in a half-Jewish city the foundling counts as a Jew, and asks what practical law that affects.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ruling says that if the city is half and half, the baby is a Jew. For what practical law does that matter?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns to the last case: a city that is exactly half Jewish and half non-Jewish. It asks the same kind of question it asked about the earlier cases: what practical difference does calling the baby a Jew make?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same pattern ran through steps 9-12, where רב פפא gave a practical result for each majority case. Now the גמרא wants a practical result for the evenly split case. This one is harder, because the baby's status is a real doubt.

keyTerms.meaning: Half and half: an even split between Jews and non-Jews
For what law? What practical difference does it make?

phrases.english: Half and half — a Jew,
phrases.notes: This quotes the ruling about a city split evenly between Jews and non-Jews: the baby found there counts as a Jew.

phrases.english: for what law [does this matter]?

steps.triggerLanguage: מֶחֱצָה עַל מֶחֱצָה — יִשְׂרָאֵל, לְמַאי הִלְכְתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the series of 'what practical law' questions, now applied to the evenly split case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical law that follows from treating the foundling in a half-Jewish city as a Jew.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: It matters for damages
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש answers that the ruling matters for the laws of damages.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: It matters for damages.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש gives a short answer: calling the baby a Jew matters for the laws of damages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the laws of damages, the payment depends on whether the owners are Jews or non-Jews. So the baby's status could change how much money is paid. ריש לקיש does not yet say which damage case he means, and the next step asks exactly that.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא from ארץ ישראל
Damages: the laws of paying for harm done

phrases.english: Reish Lakish said:
For damages.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The half-and-half ruling matters for the laws of damages.

steps.title: The case where the foundling collects cannot be meant
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what damage case ריש לקיש means, and rejects the case where the foundling's ox was gored: he could not collect without proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If you say our ox gored his ox, the owner of our ox can tell him: Bring proof that you are a Jew, and then take the money!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what damage case ריש לקיש means. It tries the case where a Jew's ox gored the foundling's ox, then shows that case does not work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the foundling is the one trying to collect, and he wants to be paid as a Jew. The Jewish owner can say: 'Prove you are a Jew first.' The foundling cannot prove it, because his status is a true half-and-half doubt. So calling him a Jew would not help him collect anything, and ריש לקיש cannot mean this case.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How do we picture it?
Gored it
Ox
Bring proof

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up who is collecting. In this case the foundling is the one who wants money, so he has to bring proof. A doubt alone does not let someone take money from another person.

phrases.english: What is the case?
If we say
that our ox gored his ox —
phrases.notes: 'Our ox' means an ox owned by a Jew; 'his ox' means the foundling's ox.

phrases.english: let him say to him:
Bring proof that you are a Jew
and take [the payment]!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests ריש לקיש's answer by trying to identify the case, and rejects the first possible case.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's statement that the half-and-half ruling matters for damages.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the foundling is the one claiming money, his doubtful status cannot help him, because the one claiming must bring proof.

steps.title: The case where the foundling's ox did the damage
steps.stepSummary: The ruling is needed when the foundling's ox gored a Jew's ox. He pays half, like a Jew, and refuses the other half unless they prove he is not a Jew.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed only where his ox gored our ox. He pays half. For the other half, he says to them: Bring proof that I am not a Jew, and I will give it to you.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that ריש לקיש means the opposite case: the foundling's ox gored a Jew's ox. Here the foundling is the one paying, so his status as a Jew protects him from paying extra.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When one Jew's ox gores another Jew's ox, the owner pays half, so the foundling pays at least that much. The Jewish owner wants the other half too, claiming the foundling is a non-Jew. The foundling can answer: 'You are the one claiming the money, so prove I am not a Jew.' His status as a Jew keeps him from paying the extra half.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for... (introduces the case where the ruling matters)
Half
He pays

steps.whatToRemember: The foundling in a half-Jewish city is treated as a Jew in a way that protects him. When he has to pay, the other side must prove he is not a Jew. When he wants to collect, he must prove he is a Jew.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows a general rule of money law: the one who wants to take money from another person must bring proof.

phrases.english: It is needed only
where his ox gored our ox,
he pays half.
And the other half —
he says to them:
Bring proof that I am not a Jew,
and I will give it to you.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא: דְּנַגְחֵיהּ תּוֹרָא דִידֵיהּ לְתוֹרָא דִידַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 15 by moving ריש לקיש's ruling to the opposite case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Case limitation: the ruling applies where the foundling is the one who pays.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might have thought ריש לקיש meant a case where the foundling collects damages as a Jew.
steps.terutzMaskana: He means a case where the foundling's ox did the damage. His status as a Jew limits his payment to half.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing בתולה נשאת
steps.stepSummary: The closing formula for the first chapter of כתובות, בתולה נשאת.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, 'בתולה נשאת.'
steps.whatsHappening: This line marks the end of the chapter בתולה נשאת. It is a closing formula, not part of the argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Learners say the הדרן at the end of a chapter to show they plan to come back to it. The discussion of the foundling ends here, and a new chapter begins next.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you: said at the close of a chapter
'A virgin is married': the name of the first chapter of כתובות

phrases.english: We will return to you, 'A virgin is married'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the chapter after the final discussion.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The first chapter of כתובות, בתולה נשאת, is complete.

steps.title: Proving she married as a virgin
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה: a widowed or divorced woman claims she married as a בתולה, and her husband says she was an אלמנה. Witnesses to virgin wedding customs prove her claim. רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה adds another proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: A woman who was widowed or divorced says: 'You married me as a virgin.' He says: 'No, you were a widow when I married you.' If there are witnesses that she went out with a הינומא and her hair uncovered, her כתובה is two hundred. רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה says: Even handing out roasted grain is proof.
steps.whatsHappening: A new chapter opens with a משנה about an argument over the amount of a כתובה. The wife says she married as a בתולה, so she gets two hundred. The husband says she was an אלמנה, so she gets less.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says she can win with witnesses to customs that were done only at a virgin's wedding: going out in a הינומא and with uncovered hair. Then her כתובה is two hundred. רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה adds that witnesses to the handing out of roasted grain also count as proof.

keyTerms.meaning: She became a widow
A special covering or canopy used at a virgin's wedding procession
Her hair uncovered, a custom of virgin brides
Her כתובה is two hundred: the amount for a virgin
Handing out roasted grain at the wedding

steps.whyThisMatters: This משנה sets up the main topic of the new chapter: when we accept someone's claim, and what counts as proof.

phrases.english: A woman who was widowed
or who was divorced.
She says: You married me as a virgin,
and he says: Not so,
rather, I married you as a widow.
phrases.notes: A widow's כתובה is smaller than a virgin's, so the argument is really about how much money she gets.

that she went out with a hinnuma and her hair uncovered —
phrases.notes: These were customs done at a virgin's wedding procession from her father's house.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new chapter after the הדרן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Witnesses to virgin wedding customs (הינומא, uncovered hair) prove she married as a בתולה, so her כתובה is two hundred. רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה says handing out roasted grain is also proof.

steps.title: רבי יהושע agrees about the field bought from your father
steps.stepSummary: The משנה states that רבי יהושע agrees a man is believed when he says, 'This field was your father's, and I bought it from him.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהושע agrees that if someone tells another person, 'This field belonged to your father, and I bought it from him,' he is believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings a case where even רבי יהושע, who usually demands proof, agrees that the speaker is believed. This sets up the reason, which the משנה gives on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man holding the field gives us two pieces of information. First, the field used to belong to the other person's father. Second, he bought it. Nobody knew the first fact without him, so we believe his whole statement, including the claim that he bought it.

keyTerms.meaning: agrees; admits that in this case the other side is right
to his fellow; to another person
a field
I bought it
believed; his word is accepted

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think he is believed only about the first half, that the field was the father's. He is believed about the whole claim, including that he bought it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This case shows an important principle. When the only source of a damaging fact is the person's own word, we also believe the part of the claim that helps them.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehoshua agrees
phrases.notes: In the previous פרק, רבי יהושע argued with רבן גמליאל and would not believe people's claims without proof. Here he agrees.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person who says 'this field was your father's and I bought it from him' is believed about his whole claim, and רבי יהושע agrees.
